blocks.raw:
<Callout>

Phenomenology redirects architectural attention from abstract form and function toward lived embodied experience, sensory perception, and the qualitative character of place. The LEA tests your understanding of phenomenological philosophy's application to architecture, particularly through Norberg-Schulz's concept of genius loci, Heidegger's "Building Dwelling Thinking," and contemporary practitioners like Peter Zumthor who design "atmospheres" rather than abstract forms.
</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Heidegger's Fourfold—**earth, sky, mortals, divinities**—is testable exactly. Don't paraphrase. Be able to recall all four and explain each: earth (materials, gravity), sky (light, weather, seasons), mortals (human presence, finitude), divinities (transcendence, meaning). A building manifesting all four authentically supports dwelling; one missing any element is deficient.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Heidegger's critique is *not* romantic anti-modernism. He's not saying "abandon technology and return to vernacular building." Rather, he's claiming that modernism's *reduction of building to technical problem-solving* eviscerates building's existential role in enabling human dwelling. The solution is not rejection of technology but technological practice *oriented toward dwelling rather than optimization*. This subtle distinction is crucial—contemporary phenomenological architects use digital tools, but in service of place-specific sensory engagement.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Common misreading: Heidegger criticizes "housing shortage"—does NOT mean housing abundance solves dwelling problem. The issue is existential, not quantitative. Thousands of modernist apartments solving the "shortage" may still fail at "dwelling" if they don't enable poetic encounter with place/materials/meaning. This is why phenomenological architecture remains relevant despite successful modern mass housing—it identifies a different kind of problem than quantitative shortage.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating Genius Loci as Purely Visual Aesthetic. Genius loci is not the scenic beauty of a landscape. It is the comprehensive character of a place—including climate, history, social patterns, material traditions, and embodied experience. A beautiful view from a distance may not possess genius loci if the place lacks rich sensory, social, or historical engagement.", "Reducing Zumthor to Material Expression. While Zumthor values local materials, his phenomenology is not simply \"use local stone.\" Rather, his work orchestrates complex sensory sequences—light, temperature, acoustic, tactile—that create what he calls \"atmospheres.\" Materials are vehicles for this orchestration, not ends in themselves.", "Ignoring the Digital Critique. Contemporary phenomenological theory emerges partly as a response to digital mediation's threat to embodied experience. Understanding phenomenology requires understanding its polemical position against virtual simulation, parametric abstraction, and screen-mediated design processes.", "Missing Phenomenology's Integration of Place and Dwelling. Genius loci is not merely aesthetic appreciation of place; it is the condition enabling authentic dwelling. Architecture's phenomenological success is measured by whether it allows inhabitants to dwell meaningfully, to feel at home, to connect with place and community—not simply by visual or sensory aesthetics."]} />
